ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: It is known that a certain restriction endonuclease has 3 restriction sites on a linear DNA molecule, as indicated by the arrows in the figure. If this linear DNA molecule is cut by this enzyme at all 3 restriction sites, four DNA fragments of different lengths, a, b, c, and d, will be produced. Now there are multiple such linear DNA molecules. If at least 1 restriction site on each DNA molecule is cut by this enzyme, then theoretically, after digestion by this enzyme, what is the maximum number of types of DNA fragments of different lengths that these linear DNA molecules can produce?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, there is a horizontal linear DNA molecule, with 3 downward arrows above it, indicating 3 restriction enzyme cutting sites. These 3 restriction enzyme cutting sites divide the whole linear DNA from left to right into 4 adjacent basic fragments, labeled in the figure in order as a, b, c, d. Reasoning: Multiple identical linear DNA molecules are cut by enzymes, and each DNA molecule has at least 1 restriction site cut, so the result can be regarded as choosing any non-empty subset among the 3 sites for cutting. After linear DNA is partially cut, the fragments produced can only be continuous combinations of adjacent basic fragments. The possible lengths include: single basic fragments a, b, c, d, 4 types in total; combinations of two adjacent fragments a+b, b+c, c+d, 3 types in total; combinations of three adjacent fragments a+b+c, b+c+d, 2 types in total. The complete four-fragment combination a+b+c+d would appear as intact DNA only when none of the 3 sites is cut, but the question states that each DNA has at least 1 site cut, so it is excluded. Counting according to the theoretical maximum and assuming these lengths are all different, the number of types is 4+3+2=9.
